title: HNSW II: M, efConstruction, efSearch
summary: Measured on a real incremental build: efSearch is a per-query knob you can change freely, while M and efConstruction are frozen at build time. Raising M past about 16 does nothing because the diversity heuristic refuses the extra edges, and a cheap efConstruction bakes a worse graph in permanently.
html:
Yesterday ended with a graph that got 0.34 and a claim that a candidate list fixes it. Today has three knobs, real numbers for each, and one distinction that matters more than all of them: one of these you can change whenever you like, and two of them you are choosing permanently.

To measure them honestly I wrote an actual incremental NSW build, insertion by insertion, with the diversity pruning from yesterday. 2,800 real document embeddings, 200 held-out queries, k=10, recall against exact search. Day 19 adds the layers.

efSearch: the one you can change

Search keeps a candidate list of size efSearch, expanding the most promising unvisited node each round rather than tracking one pointer. Bigger list, more of the graph explored, higher recall.

 efSearch  recall@10  visited  %corpus
       16      0.946      280    10.0%
       32      0.985      424    15.2%
       64      0.998      661    23.6%
      128      1.000     1027    36.7%
      256      1.000     1547    55.2%

That is Day 16's triangle again, drawn by a single number you pass in at query time. No rebuild, no restart, and you can set it per request: 32 for an autocomplete, 128 for a report that has to be right.

Note where it stops paying. Going from 32 to 128 buys 1.5 points of recall and visits 2.4 times as many nodes. Past 128 you are purchasing nothing at all.

M: the connectivity, frozen at build

M is how many neighbours each node keeps. More edges, more escape routes, better navigation, more memory.

  M  build s  avg deg  recall@10  edge bytes/vec  % of vector
  4      1.2      6.0      0.851              24         1.6%
  8      1.8     11.5      0.963              46         3.0%
 16      2.6     18.6      0.985              74         4.8%
 32      2.9     22.2      0.988              89         5.8%
 48      3.0     22.4      0.989              90         5.8%

M=4 to M=16 is worth 13 points. M=16 to M=48 is worth 0.4 points.

Look at the degree column, because it explains why. I asked for up to 48 neighbours and got 22.4. The diversity heuristic from yesterday is refusing them: a candidate only gets an edge if it is closer to this node than to any neighbour already chosen, and past a certain density every new candidate sits behind an existing edge. Raising M stops doing anything because the pruning rule will not accept the edges.

That is worth knowing before you set M=64 because a config file somewhere does. You will pay the build time and get a graph that looks much like M=24.

efConstruction: the graph quality, also frozen

When inserting a node, the builder searches the partial graph to find who to connect to. efConstruction is the beam width of that search. Low means each node connects to a poor guess at its neighbours, and that mistake is baked into the structure forever.

  efC  build s  avg deg  recall@10
    4      0.3      4.6      0.623
    8      0.4      7.2      0.856
   16      0.7     11.0      0.952
   32      1.5     15.1      0.974
   64      2.9     18.6      0.985
  128      4.5     20.8      0.990
  256      6.9     21.7      0.989

Same M, same efSearch, same queries. The only difference is how hard the builder looked while constructing, and it moves recall from 0.623 to 0.990.

Build time scales roughly linearly, 23 times from efC=4 to efC=256, and the quality saturates near 128. At 256 recall went very slightly down, which at this sample size is noise rather than a finding, but it does establish there is nothing left to buy.

The asymmetry to remember: efConstruction costs you once and costs queries nothing. It is paid in a batch job you run overnight. Being stingy with it is the worst trade on this page, because the penalty shows up on every query forever and the only fix is rebuilding the index.

Which decisions are reversible

ParameterWhen setCostsChanging it later
efSearchper querylatencyfree, change it per request
Mbuildmemory, some build timefull rebuild
efConstructionbuildbuild time onlyfull rebuild

This is the shape of decision you already know from storage: page size, block size, compression codec. Chosen at format time, lived with until you rewrite everything. And as there, the recovery path is not a config change, it is a migration with a blue/green cutover (Day 74).

They are not independent

Treating these as three separate dials is the mistake. They interact, and in one direction only.

A graph built badly cannot be searched well. If efConstruction was 8, the edges are wrong, and no efSearch rescues them: you are exploring more of a structure that points in the wrong directions, so you pay the latency and get a fraction of the recall. That is what makes build-time parameters different in kind rather than just in convenience.

It works the other way slightly. A higher M partially covers for a mediocre efConstruction, because more edges per node means more chances that one of the badly chosen ones happens to be useful. It is compensation, not a fix, and you pay for it in memory on every vector.

The practical consequence: when recall is disappointing, raising efSearch is the first thing to try because it is free and immediate. If the curve flattens below where you need it, the problem is the graph and no runtime knob will reach it.

What happens after the build

One thing the parameter tables do not show, and it bites in production. HNSW has no clean delete.

Removing a node means removing a vertex from a graph that other nodes route through, so most implementations tombstone instead: mark it deleted, keep it in the structure, filter it out of results. The node still occupies memory and still gets traversed, and over time a high-churn index fills with vertices that cost time and return nothing.

Worse, the graph was built with the diversity heuristic assuming those nodes were there. Delete enough and the carefully spread edges start pointing at tombstones, connectivity quietly degrades, and recall drops with no config change to blame. The fix is a periodic rebuild, which is the same operational pattern as compaction in an LSM tree: deletes are cheap at write time and you pay for them later in a background job.

If your corpus churns, budget for that rebuild when you plan capacity, not when recall starts sliding.

A defensible default

From the numbers above, and consistent with what the library defaults do:

  • M = 16. Past the knee, before the pruning rule starts ignoring you. Go to 32 for high-dimensional or awkwardly clustered data, which you should confirm by measuring rather than assuming.
  • efConstruction = 128 or 200. It only costs build time. Be generous.
  • efSearch = tune it live. Start at 64, sweep it against your Day 14 harness, and pick the point where your recall curve meets your latency budget.

One caveat on all of this. My corpus is 2,800 vectors of 384 dimensions. The shapes of these curves are general, the exact knee positions are not: higher dimensions and larger corpora both push the useful M and efSearch up. Treat the table as a map of the terrain and run your own sweep for the coordinates.

You now know what each parameter does and what it costs. Tomorrow you write the thing: HNSW with the layers, from scratch, and find out which parts of the paper are load bearing.
exercise:
1. Sweep efSearch on something real. If you have a vector database to hand, index a few thousand vectors and run the same sweep: ef_search at 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, recording recall against brute force and latency at each. You are looking for your own knee. It will not be exactly where mine is.

2. Prove efConstruction is permanent. Build the same data twice, once at efConstruction 8 and once at 200, with identical M and identical efSearch at query time. Confirm the cheap build is still worse no matter how high you push efSearch. That is the experiment that makes "frozen at build" mean something.

3. Price your own index. For your real corpus size and dimension, compute the edge memory at M=16 and M=32 (roughly M * 2 * 4 bytes per vector for the bidirectional links), and add it to the raw vector bytes from Day 9. If the total does not fit in the RAM you actually have, you have just discovered why Days 21 to 26 exist.
